t: defiles a person and vessels by contact. Like all primary sources of impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:7).
and earthenware vessels through the airspace. For an earthenware vessel becomes impure when impurity enters its hollow (ibid. 1:5, Hilchot Kelim 13:1).

and defiles a person by carrying, to defile clothes. For a person who carries an olive-bulk of the flesh of a carcass also defiles the clothes on him while he carries it, unlike a person who touches a carcass, as below.

like the riding-vessel of a zav. A vessel fit for riding that became impure through the zav's treading ("midras impurity," see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 7:1), which likewise does not defile a person so as to defile clothes except by carrying, but not by contact (see ibid. 6:2, below 6:12).
because it is a derivative. A derivative of impurity, first-degree impurity or lower (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:8).
and a derivative does not defile vessels. Only foods and liquids (ibid. 5:7).
he shall wash his clothes. This implies that the clothes on him are impure, and the same applies to other vessels he touches while carrying it (Hilchot Parah 5:2, and see Piskei VeShitot there).
as we explained regarding those that defile a bed and a seat. 6:2.
and the slaughter of a pure animal and a pure wild animal purifies it. For if he slaughtered them properly they do not defile as a carcass.

and even if he slaughtered unconsecrated animals in the Temple courtyard and consecrated animals outside. Although in these cases the slaughter was done in violation of a prohibition and the animal is forbidden to eat (Hilchot Shechitah 2:1-2, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 18:3), it purifies the animal or wild animal so that they do not defile as a carcass.
and if a disqualification occurred in the slaughter. That the slaughter itself was not done properly and was invalid.
as we explained in Hilchot Shechitah. 3:18.
one who stabs. Kills by drawing blood other than by slaughter, such as by stabbing and the like.

and all carcasses combine for impurity into one olive-bulk, whether impure or pure. Although with regard to the prohibition of eating, a pure carcass does not combine with an impure one (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:17).
marrow is like flesh. The marrow inside the bones defiles like the flesh of the carcass (see also Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:5).
it is like impure liquids, etc.. Like liquids that became impure, which are only first-degree impurity (for the details of the laws of the impurity of liquids see below, chapter 7).

as it says: "The fat of a carcass and the fat of a torn animal may be used". And the verse continues "for any work," and from here they learned that this fat does not defile as a carcass (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 3:9).

one whose prohibition is on account of carcass and torn animal. The verse speaks of the fat of an animal to which the prohibitions of carcass and torn animal apply, namely a pure animal, for with an impure animal and wild animal these prohibitions do not apply (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:2), and with the fat of a pure wild animal there is no prohibition of forbidden fat (ibid. 7:1, see Commentary on the Mishnah there).
and if it was rendered fit with the liquids that render fit. If it was moistened by one of the seven liquids that make foods susceptible to impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:1-2).
it is like impure foods. By the law of food that touched a carcass, which is first-degree impurity.

and one who touches the fat that covers the kidney before separation. For the animal's kidney is entirely covered with fat in such a way that it is hard to touch the kidney itself as long as the fat has not been separated from it.

for several threads of it extend through the fat. Several thin threads of the kidney extend outside the fat and can be touched; therefore one who touches the fat is like one who touches the kidney (see Meiri, Chullin 126b).

the koy. An animal that is in doubt whether it is a wild animal or a domestic animal, and therefore the stringencies of both a wild animal and a domestic animal apply to it (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 1:13, Hilchot Nezirut 2:10-11, Commentary on the Mishnah, Bikkurim 2:8).
its fat defiles like its flesh. By the law of the fat of a wild animal (but with regard to eating, its fat is forbidden by the law of the fat of a domestic animal - Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot ibid.).
therefore terumah and sacrificial food are not burned on its account. Terumah and sacrificial food that became impure through it are not burned.

and one is not liable to karet for its impurity for entering the Temple or for eating its sacrificial food. One who became impure from it is not liable to karet if he intentionally entered the Temple or ate sacrificial food.
and these are things that do not defile as carcasses. That are not considered flesh to defile as a carcass (and for their impurity as foods see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:4).
and the hooves. The horny part that covers the tips of the toes.
even their soft base which, if cut from a living animal, would produce blood. The inner part of the horns and hooves, which is like flesh in that it is soft and blood comes out of it.
even if it is not tanned. And it is still somewhat soft.
and the alal. Remnants of flesh stuck to the hide when it is flayed from the flesh (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 14:7).
and the spices. Seasonings.

but one who touches any of these while they are attached to the flesh is impure. When they are attached to the flesh of the carcass, one who touches them is defiled as if he touched the flesh of the carcass itself.
for none of these combines to make an olive-bulk. To defile as a carcass, and likewise for lashes for eating it (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:18).
the alal, whether an animal tore it off or a knife cut it off. Whether the hide with the pieces on it was torn from the rest of the flesh by an animal or cut by a person with a knife.

and if he gathered it and it contained an olive-bulk, it defiles. Since a person gathered it into one place, it is considered flesh and defiles (but not where it gathered by itself and the like, Rashi, Chullin 121a).
and these are animals whose hides are like flesh. They are soft like flesh, so they have the same law (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:21).
a domesticated pig. A pig raised among people.
hump. A camel's hump.
the place of shame. The female's private part.
the fetus. A fetus found in the womb of an animal that died.
and the hide under the fat tail. The skin on the sheep's tail where there is no hair.
he walked on them for the time needed for tanning. He trod on them with his feet for the length of time needed to tan hides.
that he made it a patch for his basket. That he used it as a patch for his basket.
pure. For the flesh in the ear lost its status as flesh and became skin, which does not defile as a carcass (Tosafot, Chullin 122b).
as long as he has not loaded it. As long as no load was ever placed on it (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:21).
its time to be loaded arrived. The camel reached the age at which loads are placed on it.
if he flayed it for a rug. One who flays the hide for a rug cuts the animal lengthwise from the tail to the neck and begins to flay the hide from both sides.
enough for a grip. The amount of hide that is convenient to grip while flaying.

he flayed it in order to make a wineskin from the hide. One who flays for a wineskin tears the hide between the two legs and flays from each side until the hide comes out whole in its circumference (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 9:3; from these words it appears that the flaying begins from the animal's belly, but from Rashi's words in Chullin 123a it appears that the flaying begins from opposite its mouth).
from its leg only. He flays the whole hide from the leg so that it comes out whole without cuts (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

and likewise one who flays a swarming creature, it is a connection until he flays all of it. This refers to swarming creatures whose hides are not like their flesh (see below 4:8), which after being flayed from the flesh are pure.
the hide on the neck. Which is flayed on its own.
for if it was slaughtered. A pure animal that was slaughtered, which does not defile as a carcass but is susceptible to impurity like other foods.

with the strip that comes out of it. A thin strap torn from the hide on the side of the flesh (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 9:4); some explain that it means a thin strip of flesh coming out of the flesh (Rashi, Chullin 124a).

because the hide with its hair protects the flesh. Something attached to food that protects it (like a peel and the like) is called a "shomer" (protector) and has the law that it becomes impure and defiles like the food itself (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 5:1-4). The same applies to the impurity of a carcass: the hide and the hair on it are considered a "protector" of the flesh and defile like it (but unlike impurity of foods, the protector does not combine with the carcass for the measure of impurity, as above, halachah 7).

when is this said? Where an animal tore it off, etc.. The hide and the olive-bulk of flesh of the carcass on it defile only when they were torn from the rest of the flesh by an animal; but if a person cut them with a knife and the flesh is spread thinly over the hide, they do not defile, because in this case the flesh is nullified against the hide.
and not by carrying. Even though the one who carries the hide carries an olive-bulk's measure at once.

for whatever does not defile as a carcass by contact does not defile by carrying. Unlike the impurity of the dead, where there can be impurity by carrying even without impurity by contact (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:11, Even Yisrael).

but two halves of olives that he skewered on a splinter, the one who carries them is impure, etc.. We do not say here that whatever does not defile by contact does not defile by carrying, for here there is no hide to nullify the two halves with regard to carrying (Kesef Mishneh, and see Piskei VeShitot).

for human joining is not a joining. Therefore the two halves do not combine to an olive-bulk to defile one who touches them, even though they touch each other (and similarly in Hilchot Tum'at Met 4:5).
this one by itself and that one by itself on one splinter ... pure. Since they do not touch each other they do not combine to defile by carrying (for the reason see Chullin 124b).

therefore the nezel of a carcass is in doubt whether it defiles, etc.. Since anything fit for a dog to eat defiles as a carcass, there is room for doubt regarding the nezel (which is liquid flesh fit for a dog to eat, see Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:1) whether it is considered the flesh of the carcass or not (Aruch HaShulchan 126:22).

if it can soak in lukewarm water for twenty-four hours and return to being moist. If the carcass becomes moist again after being soaked in lukewarm water for twenty-four hours (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:1).
and even as impure foods it does not defile. For food that became impure and afterward became unfit for a dog to eat leaves its impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 2:18).

flesh of a carcass that was rotten from the start, etc.. That rotted from the beginning and was never fit for human consumption, for example an animal whose limbs were broken while alive and whose flesh became wormy (Rashi, Bekhorot 23b).

fit for a ger. Fit for eating by a person who is permitted it, such as a ger toshav (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:4; for the definition of a ger toshav see ibid. halachah 6, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:7).
afterbirth. The sac in which the fetus is found inside the animal.
it is like excrement and dung. Things discharged from the animal's body that are not considered part of its flesh (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:5).

and if he had in mind to eat it, it becomes impure with the impurity of foods. Since most people do not eat it, it is not susceptible to the impurity of foods until he thinks of it as food (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 4:7; and see also Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 2:15).
the curd. Food remnants found in the animal's stomach.
and the milk. The milk found in the animal's udder.

pure from anything. Even from the impurity of foods, since they are not considered food but filth within the body (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:19 regarding the stomach contents, Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:23 regarding the milk in the udder; and see there that the milk in the stomach defiles with the impurity of foods if he had it in mind).
who discharged a clot of blood. Expelled a piece of blood.
even though she is exempt from the firstborn. For the presumption is that the offspring is within her (Hilchot Bekhorot 4:11).
because it is nullified by the majority that comes out with it. For most of the blood comes out with it, which destroys the stillborn and nullifies it (ibid.).

even though it was fit for a ger while on its mother's back. Although this piece was fit to defile like the flesh of a carcass, since it was fit for eating while in its mother's womb, nevertheless it is pure since the blood nullifies it.
but if he carried all of it, he is impure. For he certainly carried the carcass.

for it is impossible for a slaughtered animal to return to being a carcass, but the carcass ... therefore it will be nullified. It appears that these words refer to the beginning of the halachah, coming to explain how the impurity can be nullified by the mixture (Ne'um David, Aruch HaShulchan 127:38).
an impure animal or wild animal that was slaughtered. And its slaughter does not remove it from the status of carcass (above 1:3).
as long as it convulses. As long as it moves its limbs after slaughter, for it has not yet died completely.
stabbed it. Killed it other than by slaughter.

it has not even the impurity of foods as long as it convulses. Since it was not slaughtered, it is not considered food but a living creature, which does not become impure at all until it dies (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 2:6).

forbidden to the descendants of Noah as a limb separated from a living animal, etc.. For the descendants of Noah are commanded in the prohibition of eating a limb and flesh from a living animal, including a limb and flesh that separate from a convulsing animal (Hilchot Melachim 9:12).

and likewise a pure animal whose slaughter was invalidated. A pure animal whose slaughter was invalidated because of one of the things that invalidate slaughter (as detailed in Hilchot Shechitah, chapter 3), and it is forbidden to eat like a carcass.

he slaughtered one or the majority of one. An animal is permitted for eating by slaughtering the two organs (windpipe and gullet) or the majority of them (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9). When he slaughtered one organ or the majority of it, the slaughter is invalid.
it has no impurity at all until it dies. The animal has no impurity of foods since it was not slaughtered properly, and the impurity of carcasses does not apply since it has not yet died.
he divided the animal in two, etc.. See also Hilchot Shechitah 3:19 regarding the prohibition of eating.
or its thigh and its hollow were removed. That the animal's thigh and its hollow were removed, which is the flesh covering the pelvis.

it is a carcass and defiles by contact and by carrying even though it is still alive. For in these situations the animal is considered as if its soul left and it died, although it looks alive (see also Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:15).
or its neck-joint was broken along with most of the flesh. The vertebrae of the neck were broken, and the flesh over them was also severed.

one who touches it is pure until the stillborn comes out into the air of the world. For the stillborn does not defile while it is inside the animal's innards until it comes out of its body (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 25:12 on this law regarding a human stillborn).
the fetus. The embryo.
and limbs have no measure, etc.. A limb in its natural form, whether it separated from a living or dead animal, defiles as a carcass even though it has no olive-bulk of flesh.
like a barley grain. In the volume of a barley grain.
enough to bring up healing. Flesh in such an amount that if the limb were attached to the animal or wild animal, its flesh would heal and fill in the missing part (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:3).
or its bone was lacking. Part of its bone was missing.
and they do not make replacements. The body cannot replace them if they are lacking (unlike flesh, which fills itself in).
they are like flesh. They do not defile when they separate from a living animal.
the flesh or limb that is dangling. That are about to be torn off but are still attached to the body.
if they were rendered fit. By one of the liquids that render foods susceptible to impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:1-2).
they receive impurity in their place. Although they are attached to the animal, they are considered food and receive impurity.

if the animal was slaughtered, they were rendered fit by the slaughter. For the blood of slaughter renders the animal susceptible to the impurity of foods (ibid. 2:7), and the animal's being rendered fit also renders the dangling limb fit (for the reason see ibid. halachah 6).

for the slaughter does not make them like those that separated from a living animal. When the animal died by slaughter, the dangling limb and flesh are regarded as attached at the time of slaughter, and therefore they have the same law as the rest of the slaughtered animal, which is released from the status of carcass.

but if the animal died, etc.. Since the animal died other than by slaughter, this flesh and limb are considered as if they were torn off during its life (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 5:6, Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:6).
requires being rendered fit. By the law of flesh that separates from a living animal (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 3:3).
for flesh that separates from a limb of a living animal is pure. By the law of flesh that separates from a living animal (above, halachah 3).
and neither has a measure. Both a limb of a living animal and a limb of a carcass defile even when very small (provided that the limb is in its natural form, ibid.).

the slaughter of its mother purifies it from being a carcass. And if the mother was not a torn animal and the slaughter permitted her to be eaten, it also permits the fetus to be eaten (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 5:13).

he found in it a living eight-month fetus, and it was torn, etc.. The commentators explained that this refers to a case where its mother was not slaughtered properly (for if she had been slaughtered properly the fetus would be permitted to eat - see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 5:13; Kesef Mishneh and others). And when a disqualification occurred in the slaughter and the fetus was therefore not permitted by the slaughter ("and it was torn"), even if it is slaughtered afterward its slaughter does not purify it from being a carcass, because its species is not subject to slaughter (see Mishnah Chullin 4:4 and Commentary on the Mishnah there).
that did not live seven full days. From the time it was born.
because it is like a stillborn. Specifically where it is not known whether its months were completed (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:4).
torn animal. An animal destined to die (for the definition of this term see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:6-9).
as we explained. Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 5:14.
if its mother became impure. With the impurity of foods, after she was slaughtered.
and if its mother became a carcass. That its mother was not slaughtered properly and it is found alive inside her, and it requires slaughter.
and if it died before it spread its hooves, etc.. This refers to a case where its mother was slaughtered properly (Riko"v, cited in Kesef Mishneh).
it is pure. But if it spread its hooves on the ground, it requires slaughter and its mother's slaughter does not purify it (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot ibid.).
the limb that was cut off is a carcass. It defiles with the impurity of a carcass, like a limb that separates from a living animal (above, halachah 3, and see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 5:11).
and the rest of the flesh of the fetus is pure. And it does not become impure from the limb that was cut off.

the limb is like a torn animal that was slaughtered. That it is pure from the impurity of a carcass, for the slaughter of the mother is effective also for the limb outside to remove it from being a carcass (but it is forbidden to eat and has the law of a torn animal - ibid. halachah 9).

and the rest of the flesh of the fetus, touching a slaughtered torn animal, etc.. If the fetus was sacred, its flesh became impure from touching the limb that was cut off, which defiles sacred food by rabbinic law, as above, halachah 8.

the fetus put out its hand between the slaughter of one organ and the slaughter of the other. The fetus put out its hand precisely at the moment between the slaughter of its mother's first organ and the slaughter of the second organ.

the slaughter of one organ combines with the other, etc.. Although the second organ was slaughtered after the limb came out and was cut off, it combines with the first organ that was slaughtered earlier and purifies it from being a carcass.
standing over him. And making sure he slaughters properly.
with a good knife. One without nicks.

and likewise a Cuthean or a ger toshav, their slaughter is a carcass. For this purpose they are considered gentiles (see also Hilchot Avadim 6:6 regarding a Cuthean, Hilchot Eruvin 2:9 regarding a ger toshav).

and it seems to me that this is a primary source only by rabbinic law, etc.. Although the impurity of a carcass is everywhere a primary source of impurity by Torah law, it appears that here it is only rabbinic, for the act of slaughter itself was done properly and the animal did not become a carcass, but a gentile's slaughter is considered a sacrifice to idolatry, whose impurity is rabbinic.
offering to idolatry. What was offered to idolatry.
as will be explained. Below 6:1.

and because of idolatry the gentiles were distanced and their slaughter was forbidden. For the unspecified intention of a gentile is for idolatry (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 1:1, and see Hilchot Shechitah 2:22, 4:11-12).
and it is forbidden to eat by Torah law. Since it is considered a carcass by Torah law with regard to the prohibition of eating, why does it not also defile as a carcass by Torah law.
for entering the Temple and eating its sacrificial food. For entering the Temple or eating sacrificial food in a state of impurity, for which one is liable to karet.
the kulit of a carcass. A closed bone that contains marrow; the bone does not defile as a carcass, only the marrow inside it (above 1:4, 1:7).
for anything of a carcass that does not defile by contact, etc.. Since it is impossible to touch the marrow in the kulit, it also does not defile by carrying.
the smallest amount. Even a very small hole.

one who touches it or carries it is impure. Since he can touch the marrow with a thin object that enters the hole, the marrow is considered something that defiles by contact, and now the kulit itself also defiles like the marrow, since it is considered its protector (Rashi, Chullin 125a, and see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 5:15; for the definition of a protector see above 1:11 in the explanation).
where the marrow in it rattles, etc.. That it dried out and was uprooted from its place inside the hollow, so that the kulit cannot heal through it again.
defiles by contact and by carrying like all limbs. By the law of a limb in its natural form that has enough flesh to bring up healing, which defiles as a carcass (above, halachah 3).
and we have already explained. Hilchot Korban Pesach 10:10, Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:5.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verses.

for it is forbidden as a carcass and a torn animal. Unlike the carcass of an impure bird, which is not forbidden under these prohibitions (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:2; and see Sifra Acharei Mot, parashah 7, ch. 12, halachah 5, on how we learn that this verse does not speak of the carcass of an animal but specifically the carcass of a bird).
the swallowing place. The back part of the mouth cavity (the throat).

as it says: "and every soul that eats" - it defiles only in the place of the soul. From the phrase "soul that eats" (and not "a man who eats") they expound that it defiles only when it is in the place of the soul, which is the swallowing place.
as we explained. Hilchot Parah 5:2, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:2.
and he touched vessels at the time of his swallowing, they are impure. For that which defiles clothes also defiles the other vessels he touches while in contact with its sources of impurity (ibid.).

as we explained regarding other primary sources of impurity. For example, the impurity of the carcass of an animal (above 1:1) and the impurity of a zav and the like (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:2).
and the setting of the sun. After his immersion he must wait for evening to become pure.

the carcass of a pure bird does not require intention, etc.. Although any food not designated for human consumption requires intention in order to receive the impurity of foods (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:1), this is not the law regarding this impurity, which is a severe impurity that defiles a person and vessels; therefore one who eats it defiles clothes even if he did not think of it as food, for example if he did not know that it was this (Rashi, Niddah 50b).

if he had it in mind to eat, it defiles with the impurity of foods. For since it is forbidden to eat it, it is not considered food for the impurity of foods until he thinks of it as food, like any food not designated for human consumption (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 1:1, Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:1, and see ibid. 3:3).

and it is like a first-degree food ... and does not require being rendered fit. It defiles as impure food immediately after he thought of it, even though impurity did not touch it, and even though it was not moistened by one of the liquids that render fit to receive impurity (and see also Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 3:3; for the law of rendering fit see ibid. 1:1-2).

and the goats that are burned. The goat of Yom Kippur whose service is done inside, and the goats of idolatry (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:16), and the same applies to the bulls that are burned (see ibid. halachah 15), all of which have the status of the burned chatat offerings with regard to impurity (see Hilchot Parah 5:4).
defile the one who occupies himself with them. For one who occupies himself with burning them is impure and defiles clothes (ibid. 5:1, 5:4).
he pierced it on a spindle. He stuck it with a wooden spindle used for spinning.
into the woman's innards. Her womb.

as we explained at the beginning of the book. That this place is considered a concealed place, and although touching there does not defile, one who carries there becomes impure (Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:3, 1:8).
wrapped it in a fiber. Palm fibers tightly interwoven with each other (like a sponge).
it is pure. Since the fiber is not fit for eating, it separates between the impurity and the throat (Kesef Mishneh, and see also Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah 6:2).
does not become impure. Unlike the carcass of an animal and a swarming creature, whose limbs defile at any size (above 2:3, below 4:3).
the wings. The small feathers on the wings (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 1:2).
and the down. The fine fuzz that remains on the body after the small feathers are plucked (ibid.).
and they become impure and defile with the impurity of foods. Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:4.
the beak. The bill.
the ends of the wings. The tips of the wings.
the cluster of eggs. Eggs still attached to the hen's sinews.

the egg-cluster. Where the eggs are very small and are not yet considered eggs but flesh (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 3:7 and Maggid Mishneh there); some explain that this refers to food from the flesh of the cluster itself (Rashi, Beitzah 7a, cited in Kesef Mishneh, and see Lechem Mishneh, Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot ibid.).
who melted the fat. Melted the bird's fat.

for he made it rot. For fat melted by the sun stays a long time until it rots, and then it is not even fit for a dog to eat and therefore it is pure (below, halachah 11, and see Nazir 50a and Tosafot there).
and it cannot soak in lukewarm water, etc.. As above 1:13 regarding the carcass of an animal.

and one who eats the nezel of the carcass of a pure bird is pure. Unlike the nezel of an animal, whose impurity is in doubt (above, ibid.; the commentators discussed the reason for the distinction between the cases - see Kesef Mishneh, Melekhet Mahshevet, Chiddushei HaGriz on Nazir 50a and others).

even if it was slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. Although a bird is not slaughtered in the courtyard (whether it is unconsecrated or sacred), and if one slaughtered it, it is forbidden to eat, nevertheless the slaughter is effective to remove it from the law of carcass.

and if it was pinched and found to be a torn animal, its pinching does not purify it. Although an offering of a bird that was pinched properly does not defile, since it was found to be a torn animal and it became clear that it was not fit for the altar, its pinching does not remove it from being a carcass (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 7:3).
outside. Outside the courtyard.
and one who pinches unconsecrated birds inside. And all the more so outside.
blemishes that we explained in their place. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach, chapter 3.

atonement is written regarding it like sacred offerings. From the fact that atonement is stated in the passage of the beheaded heifer we learn that it has several laws resembling offerings (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 10:2, 10:5); therefore, like sacred animals which are purified by pinching, which is from the nape, so the heifer is purified by its beheading.
even though it is forbidden for benefit. For from the moment it went down to the valley it became forbidden for benefit (ibid. halachah 6).

and if he had it in mind to eat and it was rendered fit, etc.. Since the carcass of an impure bird cannot cause severe impurity, it requires intention and being rendered fit in order to become impure, like other foods (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 1:3, and see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 3:1, 3:3).
and the wings and the down ... are like its flesh. For with regard to the impurity of foods they have the same law as the rest of the flesh (as above, halachah 9).
as it says: "and of these you shall become impure" ... "every animal". And the verse continues: "that has split hooves."
as will be explained. Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:1.
those mentioned in the Torah. Leviticus 11:29-30.
the size of a lentil. The size of a lentil.
a limb of a swarming creature in its natural form, flesh, sinews and bone. As it was created, having flesh, sinews and bone.
whether it separated from a living one ... it defiles with its impurity. For a limb of a living one defiles like a dead swarming creature.
enough to bring up healing. An amount such that if the limb were attached to the swarming creature it would heal (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:3).
and they do not make replacements. The body cannot replace them if they are lacking (unlike flesh, which fills itself in).
they are like flesh, etc.. Since they have no bone (compare above 2:4, Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:3).

and it combines to a lentil's measure as long as it is attached to the flesh. But after it separated from the swarming creature it does not combine with its flesh to a lentil's measure, but it defiles on its own at this measure (Minchat Chinuch, commandment 159; Aruch HaShulchan 131:16). Some explain that the blood of a swarming creature that separated from the flesh does not defile on its own at all (Keren Orah, Me'ilah 17a).
and did not walk on it. Did not tread on it with his feet in order to tan it.
but the hide of the anakah, the koach, the lizard and the chomet is like their flesh, etc.. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:21.
and if he tanned them or walked on them for the time needed for tanning, etc.. As above 1:9.
the kulit of a swarming creature, etc.. See above 2:11 in the explanation.
as we explained. Above, halachah 4.

the formed egg of a swarming creature. In which an embryo began to form. And this formation defiles like a dead swarming creature (see Raavad in his commentary to the Sifra, parashah 5, ch. 7, halachah 2, and see Tiferet Yaakov, Chullin 126b, who inclined to say that it refers specifically to the formation of a dead swarming creature).
pierced it the smallest amount, one who touches it is impure. By the law of one who touches its kulit.

a swarming creature that is half flesh and half earth. A kind of mouse that grows from the ground, at the stage when it is half flesh and half earth (for the existence of such a creature see Commentary on the Mishnah and Tiferet Yisrael, Chullin 9:6).
and if it swarmed over all of it. If the fleshy half of the mouse was formed along its whole length from its head to its feet.
if it can soak in lukewarm water, etc.. As above 1:13 regarding a carcass.
and even as impure foods it does not defile. See Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 2:18.
and its skeleton. Its spine and ribs (Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 7:1, and see Hilchot Tum'at Met 3:9).
that swelled. That became swollen.
and earthenware vessels through the airspace. See above 1:1.
one who sees it from his flesh. That it came out of him.
until it comes out of him and the opening of the organ is sealed. For the drop that comes out through the male organ must reach its end and block its opening (Kesef Mishneh).

even if he saw it through a splinter, etc.. Even if the drop came out of him through a hollow splinter so that it did not touch his flesh, since it came out of the opening of the organ he became impure as one who sees semen (Rashba and other early authorities on Niddah 22a).

whether one who sees because of his flesh or one who sees by compulsion. Whether he saw because of voluntary erection of the organ or saw involuntarily, for example as a result of food or drink and the like (compare Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 2:2).
until he is nine years and one day old. For from this age on his relations count as relations (Hilchot Ishut 11:3).
and drawn out. Sticky and viscous.
for the whole of a person's body does not feel it. When it comes out of him.
without erection. Of the organ.
does not defile as semen. But as a zivah discharge it does defile in such a case (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 2:1).
was uprooted with sensation. That he felt it uprooted from its source in the reproductive organs (see Hilchot Terumot 7:4).
his flesh. His organ.
he is impure. Rabbinically (below, halachah 15).
smooth. Not flowing continuously but coming out drop by drop (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 8:2).
at the beginning. At the beginning of urination.
he is impure. For these are signs of semen.
if they were white and drawn out, he is impure. As above, halachah 3.
for the remnants of semen. Leftovers of semen.
who had relations. And now she is impure by Torah law and requires immersion (below, halachah 9).
before she wipes herself very well. So that no semen remains on her body (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 8:4).

for touching a concealed place is not touching. For the place of the genitals is considered a concealed place, and one who touches there does not become impure (Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:3, and see ibid. halachah 8).

as it says: "a man who lies with a woman". There is no such verse; it appears to mean the verse: "And a woman with whom a man lies, with an emission of semen, they shall bathe in water and be impure until evening" (see Kesef Mishneh, based on the Sifra, that the exposition is from the word "and a woman" mentioned at the start of the verse. And in the Shinuyei Nusach section of the Frankel edition they wrote that the learning is from the expression "lies," from which we learn that the woman must be fit for lying, and under three years old her relations do not count as relations, as explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:13).
not in the usual way. Relations in the rectum, from behind.
therefore. Since the woman's impurity is not due to touching but due to the act of relations itself.
even though he began. Began the act of relations.
until the man emits. Semen.
who discharged semen. That she had relations, and the semen came out of her body.
within three onot. After the time of relations, as explained below, halachah 13.

therefore she cancels one day if she was a zavah. A zavah must count seven clean days for her purification from the day she stopped seeing blood (for the definition of a zavah and the details of her laws see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:1-11). And if she discharged semen during them, that day is not counted for her (ibid. halachah 16).
like a man who saw a emission. Just as a man who saw an emission cancels one day if he was a zav (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 3:1-2).
and she defiles in any amount. For her law is that of one who sees semen, and not that of one who touches it, who becomes impure only with a lentil's measure (as above, halachah 1).
even though it did not come out, etc.. Although semen defiles one who sees it only after it leaves the body, with regard to the woman who discharges it, it defiles even while still inside.

was uprooted and reached between the teeth, she became impure, for semen is like her blood, etc.. A woman who saw blood becomes impure from it when the blood reaches the outside between the teeth even if it did not leave her body (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:2, where this place is defined), and similarly the semen she discharged defiles her even though it did not come out.
for its form has already been destroyed. And it is no longer considered semen that defiles.
and the man from whom semen separated even after several onot. For example, he was had relations with by a male and discharged the semen from his innards (Kesef Mishneh).
and the one from whom it separates is impure. The person from whom this semen was discharged is impure.
and if it can soak for twenty-four hours in lukewarm water, etc.. See above 1:13.
we have already explained in this chapter that one who sees a emission ... and likewise the woman who discharged, etc.. Above, halachot 1, 9, 11.
for example, one who has lustful thoughts and urinates. Above, halachot 5-7.
but for terumah. That they are forbidden to eat terumah and defile it by touching.

that discharged semen is impure. The semen is impure by the law of semen discharged from a Jewish woman (above, halachah 12), but the gentile woman and the animal do not become impure from it, since they do not receive impurity by Torah law (Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:13-14).
it is in doubt whether it rotted or has not yet rotted. For it is not entirely like semen discharged from a Jewish woman (for the reason for the distinction see Shabbat 86b).
we have already explained in Hilchot Metamei Mishkav. 2:10.
a gentile who felt. That the semen was uprooted from its source.

he is of doubtful impurity. For there is doubt whether we follow the uprooting, and at that time he was still a gentile and his semen was pure, or we follow the emission, and then he is already a Jew and his semen is impure (for a similar doubt see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:9).
under nine. Whose semen does not defile (above, halachah 2) and whose relations do not count as relations (Hilchot Ishut 11:3).
as we explained. Above, halachot 2, 17.
"and purify yourselves and change your garments". This implies that foreign gods defile.
and its servants. The vessels with which it is served.
and its offering. What is offered to it.
and earthenware vessels through the airspace. See above 1:1.
like a swarming creature. Like a swarming creature, which does not defile by carrying (above 4:2).

and its measure is an olive-bulk; this should not be more severe than the dead. Although it is learned from a swarming creature in the lenient direction, that it does not defile by carrying, it is not learned from it in the stringent direction to defile at a lentil's measure (ibid.), but it defiles at an olive-bulk, like the flesh of a corpse, which defiles at this measure (Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:1, and see below, halachah 3).
even if it was like an ox-goad. The size of a cattle-driver's goad, whose circumference is a handbreadth (Hilchot Tum'at Met 22:4).
as it says: "You shall cast them away like a menstruant". Said regarding idols, that they must be distanced as one distances oneself from the impurity of a niddah ("davah").

just as a niddah does not defile through her limbs. For if her hand or foot was cut off, they do not defile as a niddah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 9:1, and see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 8:4, where this sentence has an additional meaning).
and this is a greater stringency in its servants than in idolatry itself. For it does not defile through limbs (above, halachah 3).

one who puts his head and most of his body into an idolatrous temple becomes impure like one who touches. For the airspace of an idolatrous temple defiles (compare Hilchot Tum'at Met 11:1, Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 16:6).
and likewise an earthenware vessel. Which receives impurity through its airspace.
benches and chairs. Which receive impurity like other vessels, from their backs.
like a carcass. Which defiles by contact and by carrying (above 1:1).
for Scripture called them sacrifices of the dead. This is how Scripture refers to things offered to idolatry, as dead sacrifices, that is, like a carcass (and see also above 2:10).

and although the offering to idolatry of foods is never nullified so as to permit it for benefit. For idolatry, its servants, and its offering are forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:2), and if they were nullified before reaching a Jew, they and its servants are permitted, except for an offering, which is never nullified (ibid. 8:8-9).
if he nullified it. He disqualified it and profaned it from being an offering to idolatry.

but a vessel that is an offering to idolatry that he nullified is pure. Since it is possible to purify a vessel by immersing it in a mikveh, nullification is effective to purify it from impurity (Avodah Zarah 52a, and see Ran and Rashash there).

the wine of their libation is like the fat of their sacrifices. The law of wine poured out to idolatry is the same as the law of a sacrifice offered to it (and likewise with regard to the prohibition of benefit, Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 11:1-2).

ordinary wine of gentiles. Wine of gentiles about which it is not known whether it was poured out as a libation, which is forbidden to drink and to benefit from by decree of the Sages (see ibid. halachot 3-4).

defiles clothes. And the same applies to all vessels he touches while in contact with its sources of impurity, except for a person and an earthenware vessel (see Hilchot Parah 5:2 and Piskei VeShitot there).
made them first-degree. As if they had touched a primary source of impurity.
and the riding-vessel. A vessel fit for riding that became impure through the midras (treading) of a zav (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:1; 7:1).
as we explained. Above 1:1, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:2.

chatat water that has enough for sprinkling. Water of the ashes of the red heifer that contains an amount fit for sprinkling, which defiles one who touches or carries it not for its purpose (see Hilchot Parah 15:1).
and we have already explained. Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:7.
the threads of the riding-vessel. Threads that come out of it.
as we explained. Above 3:1.
he has separated from his sources of impurity. He is considered to have separated from the impurity and no longer defiles clothes (ibid.).
and the bulls and goats that are burned. The five burned chatat offerings (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:15-16).
and the one who sends out the goat. To Azazel, on Yom Kippur.
for at the time of their preparation they defile clothes. For one who occupies himself with burning them defiles clothes.
as we explained. Hilchot Parah 5:1-4.

a bed. A vessel fit for lying that became impure through the midras of a zav, which defiles by contact and by carrying, and one who touches or carries it defiles clothes (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:2).
who trod on the bed. He defiled it in one of the ways that midras impurity defiles (see ibid. 7:1).

provided that those liquids are impure because of a primary source of impurity, etc.. That the source from which the impurity came and spread to these liquids is a primary source of impurity (as below, halachah 5, unlike impurities whose source is by decree of the Sages and did not come from a primary source of impurity, as below 8:10).

a decree on account of the liquid of a zav, etc.. His saliva, semen and urine (and likewise of other sources that defile a bed and a seat), which are liquids that defile vessels by Torah law, and on account of them the Sages decreed that all impure liquids defile vessels.
as we explained. Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:14-15.

if they fell into the airspace of an earthenware vessel, all of it became impure. Even though they did not touch it at all, since an earthenware vessel receives impurity through its airspace (Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3, Hilchot Kelim 13:1).
that has an interior. A receptacle.
a vessel that can be immersed. Wooden vessels and other vessels that can be purified in a mikveh (except earthenware vessels).
only its outer side became impure, etc.. Only its outer side is considered impure, but not the inner side within it (see also Hilchot Kelim 13:4).

when is this said? Regarding terumah, but for sacred food ... all of it is second-degree impurity. For with regard to terumah the inside of this vessel is considered entirely pure and does not defile it, but for sacred food it is considered second-degree impurity and defiles it (and the law of the impurity of the outer side of this vessel will be explained below, halachot 5-6).
we have already explained. Above, halachah 1.

so that terumah and sacrificial food are not burned on account of this impurity. For impurities that are a decree of the Sages, terumah and sacrificial food are not burned (see also Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:7, Hilchot Kelim 17:5).
we have already explained, etc.. Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:8.
and all of them defile vessels. By rabbinic law (as above, halachah 2).

even if they were unconsecrated liquids. Although the outer side of a vessel that became impure through liquids is second-degree impurity (above, halachah 3) and unconsecrated food does not receive impurity from second-degree impurity (below 11:2), regarding liquids they decreed that they receive impurity even in this way.

even those who eat terumah, these are pure, etc.. Although terumah that touches a second-degree impurity is disqualified (below 11:3), the outer side of the vessel does not disqualify it, since it is considered second-degree only with regard to defiling liquids and sacred food, but not with regard to foods of terumah.
as we explained. Above, halachah 3.
only his hands became impure. But not the rest of his body, for a person does not become impure by touching a first-degree impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:7).
up to the joint. Up to the wrist joint (see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:4).

and likewise one who puts his hands into the airspace of an earthenware vessel that became impure through a primary source of impurity. For an earthenware vessel becomes impure and defiles through its airspace.
or who put his hands into a house with a plague. See also Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 16:8.

even one who puts his hands into a house with a plague. For a house with a plague is a primary source of impurity, and a person who put his head and most of his body into it became impure and became first-degree (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 16:6).

or touched with his hands a person who defiles clothes before he separated from his sources of impurity. Although this person defiles all the clothes and vessels he touches and they become first-degree impurity (see above 6:12), the hands that touched him become second-degree.
piggul and notar. Flesh of offerings that were disqualified (for their definitions see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1-3).

and the tzarir of meal offerings. A dry part of the meal offering that was not mixed with oil (Rashi, Pesachim 20a, and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 2:4, and the lexicon of Rabbi Tanchum HaYerushalmi, entry "tzard").

they are like first-degree impurity ... therefore they defile the hands with an egg's bulk. For the Sages decreed that piggul and notar defile the hands (for the reason for the decree see Pesachim 120b-121a). Regarding the tzarir of meal offerings, some explained that it refers to a meal offering that was disqualified because it lacked its oil, and it defiles like piggul and notar (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 10:17, and see Riko"v, Kesef Mishneh and others, who explained otherwise).

and piggul and notar do not combine even though their measure is the same, an egg's bulk, etc.. Generally two things that defile in the same way and at the same measure combine with each other to defile others (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:11-12). But piggul and notar do not combine to defile the hands because they have different names, and the Sages were lenient regarding the impurity of hands, which is rabbinic, that two names do not combine (Mishnah Me'ilah 4:5 and Commentary on the Mishnah there).
but other foods combine. For all foods are considered one name.
for impure foods do not defile the hands until they are an egg's bulk. See also Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:1.
the kulit of piggul. A closed bone with marrow in it.
even though it is closed. That it has no hole, and therefore one does not become impure from the marrow inside it (see above 2:11-12, 4:9).
since they became a base for a forbidden thing. Since they served as a base for the flesh of piggul or notar that was on them, they defile like it even if there is no flesh on them now (Riko"v).
that went outside its partition. Outside the boundary of the place where it is permitted to eat it (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:6).
as will be explained. Below 14:11-12.

and if it is the flesh of a Pesach offering that went outside the house. For a Pesach offering that went outside the house in which it is eaten became forbidden to eat, like sacrificial flesh that went outside its partition (Hilchot Korban Pesach 9:1-2).
the members of a group are alert. They are careful to guard it so that it does not go out, and therefore the Sages did not decree impurity on it.
as will be explained. Below 11, halachot 3-4, 7.
but for sacred food, if one hand became impure and touched the other, it made it impure. As explained below 12:12.
and both require immersion for sacred food. Immersion of the hands in a mikveh of forty se'ah with the intention to become pure for sacred food (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:5 and below 13:2).
his hands become pure by washing alone. And the laws of washing hands for terumah will be explained in Hilchot Mikva'ot, chapter 11.
because the hands are busy. And presumably they touched impurity.
and it is burned on account of this impurity. Although this impurity is only a decree of the Sages.
wrapped. Covered.
in a cloth. A sheet of fabric.
unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food or the purity of terumah. Unconsecrated food whose purity people are careful about to the level of the purity of sacred food or terumah.

because he is not careful about them. For the one who eats them does not know to be careful as the priests who eat terumah are (Rashi, Chullin 107b). Perhaps the reason is that even if they became impure they are not burned, and therefore people are less careful about them.
they made them first-degree. For even a second-degree impurity defiles liquids to become first-degree.
as we explained. Above 7:5.
for the essence of the impurity of hands is rabbinic. And only liquids that became impure through a primary source of impurity defile vessels (above, ibid., halachah 2).
until he immerses. And after he immerses he is pure and does not need to wait for nightfall (see below 9:1).

and if he touched foods, he made them third-degree. For example, where these foods are terumah or sacred food, for unconsecrated food is not made third-degree by a second-degree impurity (see below 11:2-3).
and drink with him. Together with him.
and we have already explained in Hilchot Terumot. 7:3.
half a peras, which is an egg and a half. A peras is half a loaf of bread, measuring three eggs; therefore half a peras is the measure of an egg and a half.
slightly more. A little extra.
a revi'it. A quarter of a log.
to disqualify the body. To make the person's body impure so that it disqualifies terumah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 8:2, and see also Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:3).
he ate a little and waited, etc.. And in each eating there was not the measure that defiles.

if there is from the beginning to the end the time of eating a peras. That from the start of the first eating to the end of the last eating there is the time needed to eat bread in the measure of three eggs (a peras).
he ate less than the measure and immersed and came up ... they combine. Since immersion is not required for eating less than the measure, it does not divide between the eatings.
the son is pure. Even though the milk he nurses is impure, since it came out of the body of his impure mother (see below 10:4).

a pregnant woman was permitted to eat impure foods, etc.. When a pregnant woman eats less than the measure of impure foods and waits between them, even if the total of the eatings is a large quantity, the Sages did not require immersion, not even as a stringency or as a measure of piety, so that she will not refrain from eating and endanger herself (Riko"v).
in drawn water. Water that was drawn, which is invalid for immersion (Hilchot Mikva'ot 4:1-2).
three logs. And a log is about a third of a liter (for the reason that specifically this measure defiles see Or Sameach).
and if he touched foods, he made them third-degree. In the case where they are terumah or the like (see below 11:2-3).
he defiled them and made them first-degree, etc.. See above 7:5.
but not to defile vessels. Since only liquids that became impure through a primary source of impurity defile vessels (above 7:2, 8:10).
tevulei yom. People who require nightfall after their immersion.

and they were immersing with disrespect, without intention. And one who immerses without intention is pure only for unconsecrated food but not for ma'aser sheni, terumah and sacrificial food (below 13:2, Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:8).

he does not need to wait for nightfall, etc.. He need not wait until evening to become fully pure, unlike a tevul yom who became impure from a primary source of impurity, who requires nightfall (below 10:1).
and likewise one who eats impure foods and drinks impure liquids. Who is second-degree impurity by decree of the Sages (above 8:10).
and likewise vessels that became impure through liquids. See above 7:2.
from two vessels or three ... if they fell from four vessels they do not combine. Compare Hilchot Mikva'ot 5:1.
and they fell on most of him from the side or from below. The water fell on the side or lower parts of his body, and not on the parts of the body close to his head.
wine and oil, honey and milk. And the same applies to other fruit juices (compare Hilchot Mikva'ot 7:1).
for they touched a second-degree impurity. Which makes liquids first-degree (above 7:5, and above, halachah 1).
as we explained. Above 8:1.
the straps of tefillin together with the tefillin. Tefillin defile because of the passages inside them, and the straps defile when they are attached to them.
and the margin of a scroll. The smooth blank areas of the parchment of a Torah scroll.
above and below, etc.. And the same applies to the margin between one page and the next (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 3:4, and see Tosafot Yom Tov there).
at the beginning. At the beginning of the scroll.
and a scroll in which part of the Torah is written. A sheet of a Torah scroll (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid. 3:5).

like the passage "And when the ark set out". This passage is considered a book on its own, and therefore from it they learned the number of letters that constitute a complete book (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid., and see also Hilchot Shabbat 23:28).
the Aramaic in Ezra and Daniel. The passages in these books written in Aramaic.
in Hebrew script. Ancient Hebrew script.
written in Ashurit. The holy script used for writing Torah scrolls (see Hilchot Tefillin 1:19).
for a child to learn from it. So that a child will learn from it.
even though he is not permitted. See Hilchot Sefer Torah 7:14 (and see Piskei VeShitot there).

the cords and straps that he sewed to the scroll, even though he is not permitted to keep them. Threads and straps with which he sewed the scroll, although a scroll is sewn only with sinews (see Hilchot Sefer Torah 9:13, Zer Zahav and Minchat Bikkurim on Tosefta Yadayim 2:5); some explain that he sewed them into the body of the scroll in order to tie it and the like (Magen Avraham, Orach Chayim 147, and see Chazon Ish, Yadayim 8:4).
and the case of a scroll. The ark.
and the wrappers of scrolls when they are sewn. That they were sewn specifically for the use of a Torah scroll (see Chazon Ish, Yadayim 2:12).
the blessings. A document with the text of the blessings.

books of the heretics. Holy books written by heretics or found in their possession (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:8, Hilchot Tefillin, Mezuzah VeSefer Torah 1:13), and also their compositions that contain quotations from the Torah (Meiri, Shabbat 116a).
the passage of the sotah. The scroll used to give the sotah to drink (see Hilchot Sotah 3:8-10).
as we explained. Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:8.

he is like a second-degree impurity. But he is not truly second-degree, for he does not defile others in the same way that a second-degree impurity defiles (see below, halachot 3-6); the reason is that since he immersed, his impurity is weak (see Me'ilah 8b, Commentary on the Mishnah, Introduction to Seder Tohorot).
until the sun sets for him. Until evening arrives after his immersion and three medium stars come out, about a third of an hour after sunset (Hilchot Terumot 7:2).
for example, one who immersed from zivah or from the impurity of the dead or tzara'at. For in these cases he was a primary source of impurity before the immersion and defiled people and vessels.
from the impurity of a swarming creature and the like. Who was first-degree impurity before the immersion.

whether by their rabbinic enactment. For example, he became impure from one of the primary sources of impurity that are rabbinic (for their list see Commentary on the Mishnah, Introduction to Seder Tohorot; but if he became impure from one of the other impurities that are essentially rabbinic, he does not require nightfall, as above 9:1).
disqualifies everything. That everything that touches him becomes "pasul," that is, it is itself impure but does not defile others (below 11:1).

he defiled them and they are fourth-degree. Although a tevul yom is second-degree, if he touched sacred food he made it fourth-degree, since only sacred food of the fourth degree is considered "pasul" and does not defile others (see below 11:4).

one lacking atonement. A zav, zavah, woman who gave birth and metzora who immersed and whose sun set but who have not yet brought their offerings, and are forbidden to eat sacrificial food (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
in touching sacred food they are the same. For both disqualify sacred food. But regarding terumah their law is different, for one lacking atonement is permitted terumah (below 12:15).
liquids are always first-degree. For even liquids that became impure through a second-degree impurity become first-degree by decree of the Sages (see above 7:5).
as we explained. Above 7:5.
except for a zav and his fellows, etc.. The zav and others who defile a bed and a seat, whose saliva, semen and urine are primary sources of impurity (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:14-16).
even one who eats impure foods or drinks impure liquids. Who is second-degree impurity by decree of the Sages (see above 8:10).

for a third-degree impurity in terumah ... does not defile other liquid or other food. It does not defile foods and liquids of unconsecrated food or terumah (but foods or liquids of sacred food do become impure through a third-degree impurity in terumah, as below 11:8).

and if his hands were impure, the liquid is impure. For the hands defile liquids to make them first-degree (8:10), but the pot is pure, since liquids that became impure through hands do not defile vessels (ibid.).
and this is a stringency in hands that is not in a tevul yom. And see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 7:9 for another stringency in hands compared to a tevul yom.
for a doubtful tevul yom disqualifies because of doubt. See Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 9:3.
and doubtful hands are pure, as will be explained. Below 14:1, 14:11.
as we explained. Above 8:10 and in the previous halachah.
or one who comes with his head and most of his body into drawn water. See above 9:1.
as we explained. Above 7:2-3.
we have already explained that an earthenware vessel can never be a primary source of impurity. Hilchot Tum'at Met 5:6.
chatat water. The water into which the ashes of the red heifer are put, which is a primary source of impurity and defiles one who touches or carries it not for its purpose (Hilchot Parah 15:1).

became impure by Torah law and are like first-degree impurity to defile others by rabbinic law. For by Torah law they are second-degree, which does not defile others since they touched a first-degree impurity, but by decree of the Sages they became first-degree, which defiles others.
as we explained. Above 7:5.
as we explained. Above, halachot 3-4.
as it says. Regarding the impurity of swarming creatures.
and an earthenware vessel into whose airspace a swarming creature fell is first-degree. For an earthenware vessel becomes impure through its airspace.
and the food in the vessel is second-degree. For the food became impure from the airspace of an earthenware vessel that is first-degree.
the oven. Which is an earthenware vessel.

the bread is second-degree because the oven is first-degree. Although the bread is together with the swarming creature in the oven's airspace, it does not become impure directly from the swarming creature but only because of the oven.

and from where do we learn that third-degree food is disqualified, etc.. Above 10:9 it says that this disqualification is rabbinic, so it appears that the derivation here is only an asmachta (Avraham Yagel, and see also the next halachah).
as it says. Regarding a tevul yom.
"and afterward he shall eat of the sacred things". And the Sages expounded that the "sacred things" mentioned here are terumah (see Yevamot 74b).
and if it touched it, it is disqualified. As above 10:3.

and from where do we learn that third-degree in sacred food is impure, etc.. Above 10:9 it says that this impurity is rabbinic, so it appears that the derivation here is only an asmachta (Responsa Radbaz, Alef 1557, and others).
as it says. Regarding the flesh of an offering.
and Scripture already called the second-degree "impure," etc.. As above, halachah 2.
it became impure and shall be burned. As the continuation of the verse there: "it shall not be eaten; it shall be burned with fire."
forbidden to sacred food until he brings his atonement. Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1, Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:14.
meat of desire. Unconsecrated meat.
foods joined by liquids are a joining, etc.. Foods that are joined to each other by a liquid are considered joined, so that if impurity touched one of them, the other is also impure.

and it is in doubt whether they are considered one body for counting first, second and third, etc.. There is doubt whether the two parts have the same degree of impurity and defile food that touches them equally, so that if a swarming creature touched one of them, and it is first-degree, it makes the other also first-degree, or perhaps it makes it only second-degree, which no longer defiles unconsecrated food but only terumah.
he defiled them. And made them first-degree, by the law of any second-degree impurity that touches liquids (above 7:5).

he defiled them and they became first-degree. Although terumah is third-degree, since it defiles the liquid of sacred food it makes it first-degree, by the law of any liquid that touches a second-degree impurity.
but if a third-degree impurity in terumah touched liquid of terumah, it is pure. And likewise if a third-degree impurity in sacred food touched liquid of terumah it is pure (below 12:11).
unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of terumah. Unconsecrated food whose purity people are careful about to the level of the purity of terumah.
and if it touched sacred food it does not make it fourth-degree. For in this respect its law is not that of true terumah, which disqualifies sacred food.

and unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food, the third-degree in it is pure like unconsecrated food. For unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food is not considered sacred with regard to the degrees of impurity (and in this respect its law is more lenient than unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of terumah - see Rashi, Chullin 34a). But for other matters it is considered sacred (see below 12:16).
one who eats a fourth-degree in sacred food. A person who eats sacred food that is fourth-degree impurity.

it is forbidden for him to eat sacred food, etc.. Although fourth-degree in sacred food does not defile or disqualify others (above, halachah 4), they decreed on the person who eats it that he is forbidden to eat sacred food, but they did not decree on his touching (as below, halachah 11).

even a cooked dish into which sacred food was mixed and there is not an olive-bulk in the time of eating a peras, etc.. Although the amount of sacred food mixed into this dish is small, so that there is not even an olive-bulk of sacred food in every three eggs (see above 8:11), one who ate the fourth-degree in sacred food is forbidden to eat from this dish (unlike this case regarding terumah, where it is permitted, as below, halachah 11).

but with a fifth-degree, which is pure. For a person who eats a fifth-degree in sacred food (sacred food that touched a fourth-degree) is permitted everything, since a fifth-degree in sacred food is not impure.
as we explained. Above, halachah 4.

in eating they made a stringency, in touching they did not make a stringency. For they are more stringent regarding the prohibition of eating than the prohibition of touching (for further examples see below 12:15, Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:8).
for the purity of terumah is impurity with regard to sacred food. For another law that follows from this principle see below 13:1.

for there is nothing that makes a fourth-degree in sacred food except consecrated sacred food alone. And therefore, just as they did not decree impurity on the third-degree in unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food (above, halachah 9), so they did not decree impurity on the person who eats this third-degree.
for example, the flesh of most holy offerings and the flesh of lesser holy offerings. For the definition of most holy offerings and lesser holy offerings see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:17.

and the loaves of the thanksgiving offering and the wafers of the nazirite over which the sacrifice was slaughtered. For the offerings of the thanksgiving and the nazirite require bread, and this bread becomes sanctified only after the sacrifice with which it was brought is slaughtered (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 12:14-18).
and the meal offerings that were sanctified in a vessel. For meal offerings are sanctified only after they are placed in a service vessel.

that formed a crust in the oven. That were baked until their dough hardened and was covered with a crust, and after they formed a crust they are considered sacred with regard to impurity (but with regard to disqualification the two loaves are not sacred until their two lambs are slaughtered, see ibid. 17:18).

and not like unconsecrated food but like terumah. Since they were sanctified orally by the person who brings them, they are no longer considered unconsecrated food but like terumah (see Aruch HaShulchan 144:18).
the challah and the first fruits ... are like terumah. See also Hilchot Terumot 15:20-22.
and the payments of terumah and its fifth. A non-priest who ate terumah inadvertently pays the principal and a fifth from his own unconsecrated food, and they become like terumah (ibid. 10:15).
the tevel. Produce from which terumot and ma'aserot have not been separated.
and the mixture. Unconsecrated food mixed with terumah in such a way that the mixture is forbidden to non-priests (see Hilchot Terumot 13:1-2).
and the growth of terumah. Produce that grew from terumah planted in the ground, which by decree of the Sages is forbidden to non-priests (ibid. 11:21).
and dough that is subject to challah. From which challah has not yet been separated.

anything whose certainty defiles unconsecrated food by Torah law, etc.. Dough that became impure by Torah law, the challah separated from it must be burned, and the Sages decreed that in a case of doubtful impurity, although the dough is defined as unconsecrated food, its purity must be guarded, since it was already obligated in challah and there is a prohibition to defile the challah, so that the challah separated from it will not have to be burned but will remain only in suspense (and see also Hilchot Bikkurim 8:10).
in suspense. In doubt whether it is impure or pure.
the Sages made stringencies for sacred food over terumah. Stringencies in matters of purity that apply to sacred food and do not apply to terumah.
a person may immerse vessels inside vessels. A person is permitted to place small vessels inside larger vessels and immerse them together in a mikveh.

a decree lest the mouth of the vessel be narrow and not have the size of a waterskin tube. A waterskin tube is a hollow reed placed in the mouth of a leather skin for drinking and the like, and its measure is a diameter of the width of two medium fingers (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 8:6); and where the mouth of the large vessel is so narrow that it lacks this measure, the vessels inside it are not purified (see also ibid. 3:26).

but if it was impure, since immersion worked for it, it worked for the vessels inside it, even to use them for sacred food. In a case where the large vessel is impure, even though its mouth is very narrow and lacks the size of a waterskin tube, the immersion worked for the vessels inside it (see there), and therefore in this case they did not make a stringency for sacred food and it is permitted to immerse vessels inside vessels.

a vessel whose outer side became impure through liquids, etc.. For impure liquids that touched the outer side of a vessel with a receptacle defile its outer side to make it second-degree by decree of the Sages, but its inside did not become impure (see above 7:3-4).

and not the finger-hole in the thickness of its rim. For in the thickness of the vessel there is a sunken place used for inserting a finger when holding the vessel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chagigah 3:1; the same applies to the rim-ridges and handles of the vessel, which do not become impure in this case, see Hilchot Kelim 28:1).
that is in its finger-hole. In its finger-place.
and they would again defile its inside. For if the impure liquids touched the inside of the vessel, the whole vessel became impure (above 7:3).
but for sacred food, if its outer side became impure, all of it became impure. And all of it became second-degree, which defiles sacred food (ibid.).

one who carries the midras. A vessel fit for lying or sitting that became impure and became a primary source of impurity through a zav and his fellows is called a zav's midras, and it defiles the person who carries it (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 6:1-2).

he is permitted to carry terumah with him together. For although the carrier became impure because of the midras, he does not defile the terumah as long as he does not touch it directly and as long as the midras and the terumah do not touch each other, and therefore he is permitted to carry the terumah together with the midras.
those who eat terumah. People who keep themselves pure in order to eat terumah.

their clothes are midras for sacred food. For if those who eat sacred food touched their clothes, they became impure as if they touched a zav's midras and require immersion (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chagigah 2:7, and see also below 13:1).
made of several parts. Made of multiple pieces.
he may immerse all of it at once. He is permitted to do so.
and dries. Dries each part of the dirt that accumulated on it.
vessels finished in purity. Whose making was completed in purity.
and is careful with them. That they not become impure.
and they do not require nightfall. There is no need to wait for evening for their purification.

a decree on account of the spittle of an am ha'aretz. For the Sages decreed that an am ha'aretz is presumed impure like a zav and his spittle defiles like the spittle of a zav (below 13:1, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:1).

that he touched them during the work. Before their making was completed, at which stage they do not yet receive impurity, so that even a Torah scholar was not careful to guard them from impurity (Chagigah 23a).

and it is still wet after they were finished. For the spittle of a zav defiles only while it is wet (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:1), and they were concerned that the spittle would remain wet after the vessel's making was completed and it would become impure from the spittle.

if the thing between them needs the vessel. A thing that must be placed in a service vessel in order to be sanctified (such as a meal offering, see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:12, Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:18-21; Turei Even, Chagigah 24a). Some explain it as something that must be held by a vessel so that it will not scatter (such as flour and incense, unlike meat and the like which can be held by hand; Emek HaNetziv on Sifrei Bamidbar, section 49, and see also Harchev Davar on Numbers 7:14).
and touched the second pile. An impure person touched a pile that is not connected to water.

the pure in its purity and the impure in its impurity. For a vessel combines the foods inside it only when impurity touched one of them while they were in it, but not where one of them was impure beforehand.
but in food that is sated with impurity and added nothing to it. Since the food was already impure, the touch of the tevul yom did not change its state.
as we explained. Above 11:3-4 and halachah 8 there.
one whose one hand became impure. That it touched one of the things that defile the hands (see above 8:1-4, 9:5).

disqualified the second, and it is like a third-degree. For it is not impure like other hands, which are second-degree (above 8:2), but disqualifies only sacred food (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chagigah 3:2).
mixed with liquid. Wet.
and he must immerse both. In a mikveh of forty se'ah (Hilchot Mikva'ot 9:5, and see above 8:7).
but for terumah, etc.. Above, ibid.
and even if he touched it while it was dry. But if the impure hand is wet, it defiles the other hand for terumah by means of the liquid on it (see above 8:10).
dry foods that were not rendered fit. For foods do not receive impurity until they are first moistened by one of the liquids that render them fit to receive impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:1-2).
defiled. Impure.
the love of sacred food renders them fit. Their sanctity and elevated status cause them to be fit to become impure even if they were not rendered fit by liquids.
with a spindle. With a splinter.
the onen. One who is in mourning on the day of death, who is forbidden to eat sacred food (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:6-7, Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:8-10).

for an onen and one lacking atonement are permitted to eat terumah. For an onen is permitted to eat terumah even during his period of aninut, and one lacking atonement is permitted terumah after he became pure from his impurity even if he has not yet brought his offering.
and they put their mind aside. From guarding the purity of sacred food.
and one lacking atonement who touched sacred food. Before he brought his atonement.
as we explained. Above 10:3.
the first six stringencies. Those listed above, halachot 1-6.
both for unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food. Unconsecrated food whose purity people are careful about to the level of the purity of sacred food.
for they are from the vessel, which combines what is inside it. Above, halachah 7.

therefore unconsecrated food prepared in the purity of sacred food, etc.. That with regard to the degrees of impurity they are not considered sacred, since this matter is counted among the last five stringencies (above, halachah 11).
as we explained. Above 11:9.
amei ha'aretz. Who are not expert and careful in the laws of impurity and purity.

midras for those who eat their unconsecrated food in purity. For if people who are careful to eat unconsecrated food in purity and guard against impurities touched their clothes, they require immersion as if they touched a zav's midras (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chagigah 2:7).
as we explained. Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:1.

and the clothes of those who eat their unconsecrated food in purity are midras for those who eat ma'aser sheni. For ma'aser sheni is eaten in Jerusalem in purity, and one who eats it in impurity receives lashes (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:1), and therefore its purity is more stringent.
and they are called perushim. For the meaning of this name see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 16:12.
they are not like zavim even for terumah. Although their clothes are considered midras for those who eat ma'aser, they themselves are pure for terumah.
midras for chatat. That they defile the person and the vessels that were purified for the purity of the chatat (the water of the ashes of the red heifer).
as we explained in Hilchot Parah Adumah. 13:1-2.

one who immersed without intention is pure for unconsecrated food. Even if he immersed without intention to immerse but only to cool off and the like, he is pure for unconsecrated food (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:8).
became impure through putting his mind aside. He became impure for terumah since he put his mind aside from guarding its purity.
and he does not need to wait for nightfall. He need not wait for evening in order to become pure, since this impurity is essentially rabbinic (see above 9:1).
his hands are impure through putting the mind aside. And he must wash his hands to purify them again for terumah (above 8:8).
they are busy. And there is concern that they touched impurity (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 7:8, and see the commentary of the Rosh cited in Kesef Mishneh).

he needs sprinkling on the third and seventh. Sprinkling of the water of the red heifer ashes on the third and seventh day of his purification, and afterward immersion and nightfall, as with any person impure from a corpse (see Hilchot Parah 11:1).

he requires immersion and nightfall even for terumah.
