Since he put his mind aside from becoming impure from the other impurities, his law is that of one who became impure from them with regard to terumah, and since these impurities are essentially Torah law, this immersion requires nightfall even though it is rabbinic (see above 10:2).
even in the deserts. Where people are not so common.
perhaps they became impure through a zav or a corpse. And therefore they require sprinkling on the third and seventh (see also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 11:12).

perhaps this spittle is spittle of a zav and the like. For the spittle of a zav and other sources that defile a bed and a seat is a primary source of impurity that defiles by contact and by carrying, and the same applies to spittle that is found.
even if they were found on the way down to the place of immersion. That from their location it is evident that they fell on the way to the mikveh, so that it is reasonable to say they are impure.
except for the knives for slaughtering sacred offerings. Knives used for slaughtering offerings in the Temple.
on the fourteenth of Nisan. The day of the slaughter of the Pesach offering, when all knives are presumed to have been purified for slaughtering the Pesach.

and even if the fourteenth fell on Shabbat. And we do not worry lest the knife be impure and the offering be disqualified, and he would be desecrating Shabbat (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 8:3).

for the presumption of all vessels on a festival is that they are pure. Since sprinkling and immersion are forbidden on a festival, everyone purifies his vessels before the festival (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
sprinkles on it. The water of the red heifer.

because they treated it on this day as though the thirteenth were its seventh. Since the day of slaughter is the next day, it is possible that today is the seventh day of this knife's purification, and therefore it requires sprinkling and immersion as with a person impure from a corpse on the seventh day (see Hilchot Parah 11:1).
like the other spittle found anywhere. As above, halachah 4.
for all of Israel are pure on the festival. See also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 11:9, Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 16:10.
but they leave it in suspense. They leave it undecided.
but for a doubt of a doubt. For example, a doubt of touching an impurity that defiles by doubt (below, end of halachah 13).

a beit ha-peras. A field in which a grave was plowed, in which one who walks or touches its dust becomes impure out of concern that there is a bone the size of a barley grain from a corpse, which defiles by contact and by carrying (Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:16, 10:1-2).

earth that comes from the land of the nations. A clod of earth from outside the Land of Israel, which one who touches becomes impure out of concern that it contains a bone of a corpse (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:16, 11:1-3).
clothes of an am ha'aretz. Above, halachah 1, and see also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:1.
and about vessels that are found and spittle that is found. Above, halachah 4.

and about the urine of an impure person mixed with the urine of an animal, etc.. The urine of a zav and the like is a primary source of impurity and defiles by contact and by carrying (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:14-15). When it is mixed with pure liquids so that its appearance is nullified in the mixture, everything is pure (ibid. 2:6). But where the mixture has half impure and half pure equally and it is not known whether their appearance was nullified or not, they defile out of doubt (Commentary on the Mishnah, Tohorot 4:5).
for the dead and the zav are impure by Torah law. And all six of these defile out of concern for the impurity of the dead or of a zav.
and it is third-degree to one of them. For example, it touched foods that touched a vessel or a person who touched them, and the like.
as we explained. Above, halachah 12.
doubt of drawn water for a mikveh, etc.. See also Hilchot Mikva'ot 10:1.

three logs of drawn water that fell into the mikveh disqualified it. Water that was drawn is invalid for immersion by rabbinic law, and if three logs of it (about 900 ml) fell into a mikveh that lacks forty se'ah, they disqualified it (ibid. 4:2, 4:6).
even if there is only enough room for a person and the impurity. So that it is very likely that the impurity touched him.

and all that hang or are dragged are like those that are resting. A swarming creature that is hanging or being dragged, although not fixed in place, has the law of something resting and not floating, and if there is doubt whether they touched it, its doubt is impure.

and even if a carcass or the flesh of a corpse beneath it dissolved. That they dissolved and became liquid, so that it seems that they are now part of the water and the swarming creature floats on them and is not resting.
for its doubt in a private domain is impure. For an impurity resting in a private domain and in doubt whether it was touched, its doubt is impure (but in a public domain it is pure).
as will be explained. Below 15:8, and see also below 16:1-2.
chatat water. Water of the ashes of the red heifer, which is a primary source of impurity (see Hilchot Parah 15:1).

this is in doubt whether it is like something resting or not like something resting. Since it is not clear whether the chatat water is considered something that separates between the swarming creature and the water, or whether, since it is entirely liquid, it has the law of water and does not intervene; and in addition it is possible to say that since it is impure, it is considered together with the swarming creature as a thick impurity floating on the water (see Tosafot, Nazir 64a).
therefore it seems to me that its doubt is pure. Since it is a rabbinic doubt (see Kesef Mishneh).
a basin. A bowl.
wrapped in fiber or paper. Wrapped in threads or papers, which do not receive impurity.
and the paper unfolded. The wrapping was opened.

a swarming creature found floating on top of a pit in a winepress. The wine produced in the winepress is collected in a pit, and the swarming creature was found floating on the surface of the wine in the pit.

for terumah its doubt is impure. For the terumah wine taken from this pit is considered impure, since we say that the swarming creature was there when it was taken (Gra's commentary on Tosefta Tohorot 11:9; and we do not purify on account of doubtful floating impurity, since regarding the terumah wine it is of no significance that the swarming creature is floating, but the doubt is when the swarming creature fell into the pit, and in this case the doubt is impure as below 17:3; see Tosefta Sofrim Rishonah there, p. 105).

and for the workers its doubt is pure because it is a floating impurity. Although all the wine is impure, the workers working in the winepress are pure, since for them the doubt is whether they touched the swarming creature or not, and this is a doubt of floating impurity, which is pure (Tosefta Sofrim Rishonah there).
and on its top are impure liquids. That the stick is wet on its upper side.
perhaps the liquids touched the loaves. And defiled them, for impure liquids are always considered first-degree by rabbinic law and defile foods (above 7:5).
and likewise if he is in doubt whether impure liquids touched this vessel, etc.. For impure liquids defile vessels by rabbinic law (above, ibid., halachah 2).

and likewise if he is in doubt whether these impure liquids touched other liquids, etc.. For impure liquids always defile other liquids by rabbinic law, for they do not count first and second in them (ibid., halachah 5).
or he threw an impure loaf. Which is first-degree, and defiles the liquids.

and the impure person stretched his hand into its airspace, etc.. And the impure person's hand did not touch the jar itself but only entered its airspace. And although an earthenware vessel receives impurity through its airspace, a limb of an impure person does not defile through the airspace (Or Sameach, based on Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 8:4).
and the jar is pure, for a doubt of liquids does not defile. For if the liquids were certainly impure they would certainly have defiled the jar by rabbinic law (above 7:2-3).

for they become impure only from the jar. Although the pure liquids are together with doubtfully impure liquids in the airspace of an earthenware vessel, the impurity passes to them only through the jar, and since it is pure they too are pure (Kesef Mishneh, and see above 11:2 and the explanation there).
and if these doubtful liquids were mixed with the liquids in the jar, etc.. Since they were mixed with them, all the liquids became impure out of doubt.
one who sprinkles his house with impure water or sprinkled it. Who sprays impure water or sprinkles it on the floor of his house so that dust will not rise. J.
for a doubt of liquids defiling is pure. Even with regard to terumah.
as will be explained. Below 15:8, 16:1-2.

and there are here no liquids but a loaf that is in doubt impure or pure. For as long as the liquids are recognizable on the bread, one can discuss whether they are impure or pure, and therefore their doubt is treated leniently. But after they were wiped off and cannot be recognized on it, it is impossible to be lenient, and their doubt is impure like other doubts in a private domain (Rash, Tohorot 4:9). Some explained that the reason the bread is impure is only because of appearance (see Raavad).
and before him were two impure loaves. Which are first-degree and defile the hands (see above 8:1).
and before him were two pure loaves. Of terumah, which are disqualified by second-degree hands (halachah 8 there).
and he immersed them or washed them. He immersed them in a mikveh for eating sacred food, or washed them with a vessel for eating terumah (see above 8:7).

in doubt whether the water with which he purified them is valid for hands, etc.. For the details of the things that disqualify the water, their measure and the law of intervening substances in them see Hilchot Berakhot 6:4-10 (and see also Hilchot Mikva'ot 11:2, 11:11).
in doubt he ate impure foods ... he is pure. For all these are impurities that the Sages decreed (above 8:10, 9:1).

and likewise one who eats suspended terumah. Terumah that became impure in one of the doubtful cases for which terumah is not burned but is left in suspense; although it is forbidden to eat it, the one who eats it does not become impure.

and likewise anything similar to these, derivatives of impurities that are rabbinic, its doubt is pure. For anyone who became impure out of doubt through something that is a derivative of impurity (first-degree and below) by rabbinic law is pure.

but a primary source that is rabbinic. For example, the impurity of gentiles and idolatry (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:10, above 6:1; for the list of primary sources of impurity that are rabbinic see Commentary on the Mishnah, Introduction to Seder Tohorot).
unless the primary source itself was impure out of doubt, such as a beit ha-peras and the land of the nations. For the essence of the impurity they decreed on them is because of the doubt.
as we explained. Above 13:13.
for doubtful impurity arose in their purities. That their pure unconsecrated food became impure out of doubt.

for example, the woman who has doubt of five discharges or doubt of five births. It is not known whether she is obligated in offerings for them (for examples of doubtful zivah see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:19-20, and for doubtful birth see ibid. 10:2).

and the rest are not an obligation on him. The one lacking atonement need not bring the other offerings, for since he is obligated in them only out of doubt, it suffices for him to bring one offering to purify him for eating sacred food.
as we explained in Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah. 1:10.
before it is subject to impurity, its doubt is pure. As long as the plague has not been finally determined as impure ("confirmed as impure"), it is not confirmed in a case of doubt.
as we explained in chapter six of Hilchot Nega'im. Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 6:5.
doubt of standing and passing, etc.. See also Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 10:12.

a metzora who was sitting under a tree, etc.. The seat of a metzora is impure, so when the metzora sits or even stands under the tree, the tree becomes the metzora's seat and defiles everyone who passes under its branches.

in doubt whether the metzora stood and the pure person became impure, or he did not stand. For as long as the metzora does not stand in his place the tree does not become a seat for him, and the pure person does not become impure.

it was walking with it and touched the loaves, in doubt alive or dead. The swarming creature in the weasel's mouth certainly touched the loaves, but there is doubt whether at the time it touched them it was dead or alive, in which case it does not defile.
when is this said?. That when there is doubt whether the swarming creature that touched the loaves was alive or dead, its doubt is pure.
when it took it and went away. After it passed over the loaves, and it is not known whether the swarming creature is alive or dead.

but if it was found dead in its mouth, the loaves are impure. For all impurities are as at the time they are found (above, halachah 6), and we assume it was dead at first (Gra's commentary on Tosefta Tohorot 4:4).
they saw it alive in its mouth. They saw that it was alive while in its mouth, before it went with it over the loaves.
even though they found it dead before it. Afterward.

they were pecking with them on the ground, they are like resting things. Although the peckers move the swarming creature or carcass or lift them slightly in their mouths from time to time, they are considered resting in a fixed place (like a dragged swarming creature, which is considered resting in its place, above 14:3; Tiferet Yisrael, Tohorot 4:3).

and they defile retroactively out of doubt if they were in a private domain, as will be explained. Since the impurity is judged as resting, when it is in a private domain its doubt is impure by the law of doubtful impurity in a private domain (below, halachah 8), and in this case it also defiles retroactively, and all the pure foods that were there from the time the swarming creature and carcass were found in that place are impure out of doubt, as below 18:4.
an impurity that is resting in a public domain ... was resting in a private domain. For the definition of public domain and private domain with regard to impurity see below, chapter 20.

and all these doubts that the Sages purified, even in a private domain, because they have no mind to be asked, as will be explained. Although generally a doubt in a private domain is impure, there are cases of doubt in a private domain that the Sages purified (as will be explained in the following chapters), because these are cases of doubt that have no mind to be asked, as will be explained below 16:2 (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Mishnah Achrona, Tohorot 4:7, Keren Orah, Nazir 64a).
or he moved one of them ... if the impure thing defiles by carrying. For moving is included in carrying (Hilchot Tum'at Met 1:7).
a swarming creature found burned. For example, where its skeleton does not remain, so that it does not defile at all (Niddah 56a, and see above 4:12).

and likewise a cloak found worn out. A cloak known to have been a primary source of impurity (for example, it became impure through a corpse or midras) that was found worn in such a way that it is now pure of its impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 22:16).
and a needle found broken or rusty. Known to have been impure and now broken or rusty so that it is pure of its impurity (see ibid. 11:14-16).

he is believed about himself ... and let him be concerned for himself. He is believed only for himself and is considered pure, but for others he is not believed and is considered impure, and even regarding himself he should initially be stringent and purify himself (Rash, Tohorot 5:9, Avraham Yagel). Some explain that when he says "I am pure" he is believed even to others, since his intention is explained as meaning that he immersed after they saw that he became impure (compare Hilchot Nezirut 9:17, Hilchot Shegagot 11:8), but others do not give him purities, and even he himself should be concerned and immerse lest he mistakenly think he immersed (Tiferet Yisrael, Tohorot 5:9; and see Mishnah Achrona there, Chazon Ish, Tohorot 6:13).
for the community makes the Pesach offering in impurity when the impure are the majority. See Hilchot Korban Pesach 7:1.

if certain impurity is set aside for them, all the more so for doubtful impurity, since the prohibition of all doubts is rabbinic. If the Pesach offering, whose prohibition to make it in impurity is by Torah law, is set aside for the community, all the more so doubtful impurity, whose prohibition is only rabbinic, should be set aside in a public domain, which is a public place and where the doubt of impurity concerns the many (see Chiddushei Rabbi Shimon Shkop, Ketubot, section 8).
as we explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah. 18:17.

for a sotah who was secluded, etc.. A sotah is a woman whose husband warned her before witnesses not to be secluded with a certain man and she was secluded with him, and because of the doubt that perhaps she had relations with him she is forbidden to her husband until she is tested by drinking the bitter, cursing waters (Hilchot Sotah 1:1-2). And this doubt is in a private domain, for the possibility of seclusion exists only in a private domain.
the blind. One who cannot see.
its doubt in a private domain is impure, etc.. For although they cannot see, since they have a mind their doubt in a private domain is impure.
where the matter was balanced. Where neither side of the doubt is stronger than the other.

an impure child found next to the dough with the dough in his hand. And it is not known whether the child cut from the dough with his hand and defiled it, or perhaps a pure person cut and gave it to him.
for it is the way of a child to pat, and this is its presumption. Since it is a child's way to play with dough and pat it with his hand, this is considered a presumption and the dough is impure.
and they do not burn. Terumah and sacrificial food.
and the place of their biting is found in the dough. Marks of their biting are visible on the dough.

and between the liquids and the dough is enough for it to lick its tongue. In the distance between the liquids and the dough there is enough time for the cow to lick the liquids on the edge of its mouth with its tongue.
they leave it in suspense. They leave it undecided, neither eating nor burning.
and frogs. That are not among the eight teeming creatures that convey impurity (above 4:14).
thrown away. Discarded.
and it is uncertain whether they touched or did not touch when he wrapped himself. There is concern that the cloak became impure from the impurities and touched pure foods and made them impure.

for in a case of doubtful impurity arising through human action, they are questioned etc.. Since the doubt here results from a person's action, it is considered a doubtful impurity involving something capable of being questioned, which is impure in a private domain (above 5:2).
and if it is impossible that he did not touch. It is almost certain that the pure foods became impure.
it is doubtfully impure. Even in a public domain.
on the shelf. A board fixed to a wall, like a shelf.
and a midras lies beneath it. For example, an impure garment that conveys impurity to terumah.
even though it is on a slope. The midras lies at an incline, so that if the loaf fell on it, it would not stay on top but would roll off and down (Kesef Mishneh, based on Tosafot, Niddah 4a).
for I say that a person came, took it, and placed it in this place. And we assume that this person was pure (see the reason in Responsa of the Rambam, no. 343).
beside a cemetery. The grave conveys impurity by contact and by ohel (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:15).

even though there are no lilies except in the place of the impurity. Since the lilies grow right next to the grave, it is reasonable to say that the child picked the lilies from there and became impure.
his vessels are pure. The vessels on the donkey's back.
because his father is questioned about him. This is like a doubtful impurity arising through the action of a person who is capable of being questioned, which is impure (above 5:6).
its doubt in a private domain is impure. Even though a child is not capable of being questioned, and when he is alone, even in a private domain, his doubt is pure.
and the Sages stated four doubtful cases regarding a child. According to four different stages of his development.
and she embraced him. She hugged him.
the child began to go out and come in. That he is able to walk on his own.
and they are not midras like the other garments of amei ha'aretz. For the garments of an am ha'aretz are considered midras with regard to pure foods (above 13:1).
and even though they are pure, pure foods are not prepared on them. We do not rely on their purity at the outset.
to guard his body. From becoming impure.
they eat on the strength of his body. That if pure foods touched his body (not his hands), they did not become impure.
knows how to guard his hands. That he knows to be careful about the impurity of the hands (and one who knows how to guard his body and his hands are considered as one regarding the four stages).
unconsecrated food in the name of terumah. They give him unconsecrated food but tell him it is terumah, to see how he handles it.
if there is doubt whether it overshadowed the person etc.. For an olive-bulk of flesh of a corpse conveys impurity by ohel.

the person is doubtfully impure. Even though an impurity that does not rest in its place has a pure doubt (above 15:6-7), this rule does not apply to the impurity of ohel (Babylonian Talmud, Nazir 64a).
provided that he is capable of being questioned. That he is not a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor (above 16:2).
and the vessels are pure because they are not capable of being questioned. Therefore their doubt is pure even in a private domain (ibid.).
and likewise one who fills from a vessel and pours into ten vessels. He fills a vessel with water and pours from it into ten vessels.

it is impure and all of them are pure, even though all of them are doubtful, perhaps the creeping creature was in the vessel from which he filled originally. Even though regarding all the vessels there is a doubt whether they became impure, since it is possible that the creeping creature was originally in the vessel from which he filled the water and made impure all the liquids that passed through it, which in turn made impure all the vessels into which they were poured, nonetheless only the vessel in which the creeping creature was found is impure.
rims. The neck of the vessel or a bent-over lip (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 25:6; Rashi, Niddah 3b).

since it is possible that the water flowed out and the creeping creature remained in it, all of them are impure. When the vessel from which he filled has a rim, the creeping creature can remain in it for a long time, and therefore it is more likely that the creeping creature was in it originally and afterward fell into the vessel in which it was found.

and likewise one who fills with ten buckets one after another... and it is not known which is first and which is last. He filled ten buckets with water and poured each of them into a different vessel, and it is not known which bucket filled which vessel.

and if the buckets have rims, all the buckets and all the vessels are impure. Since the buckets have rims, there is concern that the creeping creature was in one of the buckets and from there fell into the vessel in which it is now found, and since it is not known with which bucket he filled the vessel in which the creeping creature was found, all the buckets are impure. As for the other vessels, the commentators found it difficult why they are impure, since regarding them there is no concern at all that a creeping creature was in them or in the bucket that filled them (see Mirkevet HaMishneh, Chazon Nachum on Tahorot 4:4, and Aruch LaNer on Niddah 4b, who resolved this in various ways).
one who pours. Pours out.

the upper one is pure, and we do not say that it fell from the upper one etc.. For example, where the upper vessel has no rims, and therefore there is no concern that the creeping creature lingered in it at the time of filling (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
a basket. A large basket.
if it has a base or rims. If it has a bottom or a bent lip and the like, so that the dead creeping creature can remain in it for a long time, even when it is carried around.
even if it was checked and covered. Even if they checked that there was no creeping creature in it before putting the pure foods into it, and covered it immediately afterward.
all of them are impure. Even the pure foods that were taken out of the basket before he moved it to this corner.
because we presume that impurity moved from place to place. Although the impurity was found only in this place, we assume it was already in another place beforehand.
to suspend but not to burn. That we do not burn these pure foods, but leave them undecided.
one who ladles out the pit. Draws wine or oil from it.

and the creeping creature was found in the first one, all of them are impure. For even if we say that the creeping creature was only in the first barrel and did not fall into the large pit, nonetheless all the wine in the pit became impure when he lowered the barrel into it, and therefore all the wine is impure.
he was ladling with a vessel and putting into the barrels until he filled them. He draws wine or oil with a vessel and fills the barrels from it.

therefore, if he was checking each barrel... and the creeping creature was found in one of them, all of them are impure. Since he checked and covered each one of the barrels, one must say that the creeping creature was in the pit and was poured with the wine into one of them during the filling, and he did not see it.
one who picks olives from the pile. He takes olives from the place where they are heaped to soften.

if one was found in the pile, the pile is impure. The olives in the pile are impure, but the olives on the roof are pure (based on Tosefta, Tahorot 11:1, and see Kesef Mishneh and Tosafot Yom Tov on Tahorot 9:9). Some emend here: "if one was found in the roof pile, it is impure," in line with the Mishnah in Tahorot 9:9 (Chiddushei Maharich there, and see also Mirkevet HaMishneh).

if one was found between the wall and the olives, the olives are pure. If the creeping creature was found between the wall of the house and the place where the olives lie, there is no concern that it was on the olives and fell from them.

if the creeping creature was found inside a clump of olives. Olives that stuck together and became a clump, and a creeping creature was found buried inside it; in such a case it must have been there when the clump formed, and did not arrive there afterward.
perhaps they gathered on the roof and became a clump within the three days. But in less than three days they cannot become a clump (Rabbi Shimshon, Tahorot 9:9).
one who pinches off a piece from the dough and a creeping creature is found in the piece. He takes a piece of dough and found a creeping creature together with the piece.
if it was found inside the piece, the dough too is impure. When the creeping creature is found inside the dough, it surely came from the dough.
for its pit was found etc.. The pit conveys impurity only when it is attached to food, not when it is by itself (see Hilchot Tumat Okhalin 5:13, 5:17-18).
even though there is no moist liquid on it. That there is no moisture on the pit, so there is no trace of food remains that were on it previously.

and dissolved inside the loaf. Since the pit is found inside a baked loaf, one must say that it was there when the loaf was baked and hot, and the impure food dissolved within it (Chazon Ish and Torat Sefer Rishonim, Tahorot 4:10).
these are pure, even though there is liquid on it etc.. For it can be said that the liquid came from the cold dish or from elsewhere (Chazon Ish, ibid.).

and its pit was found in the house. For example, where the pit is found in a place where we assume that the food that was on it melted away, so that if it came from impure food it conveys impurity to the pure foods it touches (as above 5:6, and see Tosefta, Tahorot 4:10).

meat found in it, we follow the majority. If most of the butchers are Israelites, it is slaughtered meat and pure; if most of the butchers are gentiles, it is carcass meat and impure (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Makhshirin 2:9).

this is the rule: for what is found, follow the majority. In contrast to a doubt regarding a fixed item, where we do not follow the majority but it is considered an evenly balanced doubt (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 8:11-12).
a woman gathering a heap in the courtyard. Collecting a pile of straw and the like from the field.
for a creeping creature does not convey impurity by carrying. And since it was found inside the heap, there is no concern that she touched it.
one who sifts with a sieve. Strains food with a vessel designed for it.
was found on top of the sieve. For the way of a woman who sifts is to touch there.
as we have explained. Above 15:8.
to the alley. A lane into which several courtyards, with houses in them, open.

impurity in the house, and it is uncertain whether he entered the house or did not enter. This is a different case, where the impurity is in the house and there is doubt whether he entered the house from the alley through the courtyard.
and even if he entered etc.. This refers to both cases: when the impurity is in the courtyard and when the impurity is in the house.
the bones of a corpse. Which convey impurity by contact and carrying, and sometimes also by ohel (see Hilchot Tumat Met 2:8-10).
and the bone of a carcass. Which does not convey impurity at all when it is not attached to flesh (above 1:7).

and clods from a beit haperas or from the land of the nations. A clod of earth from a field in which a grave was plowed, or from the soil outside the Land of Israel, which convey impurity by contact and carrying by rabbinic decree (Hilchot Tumat Met, ibid., halachah 16).
an olive-bulk of a corpse. Which conveys impurity by ohel (ibid. 2:1).

two paths, one impure and one pure. For example, one of them passes through a cemetery, or a corpse lies across one of the paths, making impure all who pass on it (as below, halachah 3), and both paths are in a public domain.
one who finds a corpse lying across the width of a road. After he has already passed along this road.

if it was whole... he is impure with regard to terumah, because the presumption is that he touched. Only with regard to terumah is he impure because of this presumption, but with regard to the impurity of a nazirite and one who prepares the Paschal offering he is considered pure (see Hilchot Nezirut 9:18-19, Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:11).

and if there was a grave across the entire width of the road, the grave combines it, and one who passes there is impure. Since the entire grave conveys impurity by ohel (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:16), even one who passes opposite the empty part is impure because of the impurity of the grave (Tosafot, Nazir 63b).
for this is not like the other doubtful cases. Which are pure in a public domain.

it conveys impurity retroactively until the time he says, "I checked this alley" etc.. The pure foods that were there from that time onward are impure, out of concern that a creeping creature fell there immediately after the check (see also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 3:7).
he swept it. Cleaned it.
that he found dry. For example, where its skeleton is intact, in which case it conveys impurity even though it is dry (see above 4:12).
as we have explained. Above 13:4.
or moved it. Spittle on which they decreed impurity conveys impurity by carrying, like the spittle of a zav (see there, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:14).
we suspend the terumah because of it, since these are two doubts. We do not burn terumah because of two doubts, but only suspend it (above 13:12-13).

if they were dry and lying there. That they dried in such a way that they do not stick to the body of a person who touches them (that is, they did not dry out too much, for otherwise they do not convey impurity; Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Tahorot 4:6, and see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:1).
if he carried one of them, we suspend. As with two spittles in a private domain, as explained in the previous paragraph.
for once he carried it, it is not lying in a public domain. For it is now on the person, who is considered a private domain (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
and it stuck to him. It adhered to him.
we have already explained. Above 13:13.
anywhere. Even when it became impure in a public domain.

like a beit haperas and the like, over whose certain touch we burn in every place. One who certainly touches one of the six impurities enumerated above (ibid.), we burn terumah because of him, even though their impurity is only due to doubt.
for his spittle we burn the terumah. In a case where he touched spittle that is impure because of the decree regarding spittle that is found.

and for his garments we follow the majority. In a case where they trod on his garments, we follow the majority of the people of the city, who did not decree impurity on an ordinary person passing in the marketplace.

if most of the city is impure, his garments are midras. That they are impure with midras impurity, like garments on which a zav and the like trod (as detailed in Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav, chapters 6-7).

and he found it in a private domain, it is impure with midras impurity and impure with the impurity of a corpse. For there is doubt whether it became impure, and a doubtful impurity in a private domain is impure.

if it was lost during the day and he found it that same day, it is pure. Although the Sages decreed that vessels found in marketplaces and streets are presumed impure (above 13:4), what is said here is not included in that decree, because the vessel was found by its owner and it is known that it was pure before it was lost, and the concern is only that it became impure while lost (see Mikdash David, Tahorot sec. 47, letter 2).

if it was lost during the day and he found it at night... it is presumed impure. Because at night an impure person treads on it without seeing it (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Tahorot 8:3, which implies that it is impure only with midras impurity, and this is also the view of the Ra'avad; and see Kesef Mishneh and Tosafot Yom Tov there).
or he forgot it in a public domain. That he knew the vessel was there and did not lose it, but forgot to collect it.
one who spreads out vessels. He spreads out his garments to dry them.
as we have explained. Above 5:7.
mentally incompetent. A woman who does not know how to guard herself and keep the laws of niddah.
or a gentile woman. Whom the Sages decreed to be considered like a zavah, and her spittle is impure (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 2:10).

all the spittle in the city is presumed impure forever, everywhere. Although the Sages decreed that spittle found in marketplaces and streets is presumed impure and terumah is burned because of it (above 13:13), in a case where there is a mentally incompetent or gentile woman in the city, even the spittle in houses, courtyards, and the like is presumed impure (Chazon Ish, Tahorot 6:10; Mishnah Achronah, Tahorot 5:8; and see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah and Rosh there).

or she sat with him in a ship. For example, a small ship that tilts when a person boards it; one who sits in it with a zav and the like has garments that are doubtfully midras-impure, even though their garments do not touch each other (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 9:4).
if she knows him to be one who eats terumah, his vessels are pure. For if she were impure, she would have been careful not to tread on his garments or board the ship with him.
and if not, he should ask her. Whether she is impure or pure.
for all impurities are as of the time they are found. Since he found in the morning that he is dead, it should be assumed that he was already dead at night as well.
one who is dying. A dying person.
a drop. A drop of spittle.

because the edge of the pit absorbs. The drop is absorbed by the edge of the pit and does not make impure what is inside (unlike oil, which, being slippery, lets the drop slide from the edge of the pit into it; Rabbi Shimshon, Tahorot 10:6, cited in Kesef Mishneh).
two paths. Which have the law of a public domain.
one impure. For example, a corpse lies across one of the paths, making impure all who pass on it.
and prepared pure foods. He touched with his hands terumah or consecrated items that require purity.

and was sprinkled on the third and the seventh, immersed, and became pure. The waters of the red heifer were sprinkled on him on the third day and the seventh day, and at the end he immersed and waited for nightfall, as one is purified from the impurity of a corpse (see Hilchot Parah 11:1).
these are pure. For they are in doubt, and a doubtful impurity in a public domain is pure.
we rule for each one of them individually that he is pure. For regarding each of them we presume that the other is the impure one, since a doubtful impurity in a public domain is pure.

both are impure and the pure foods they prepared are burned. The commentators found it difficult why the pure foods are burned and we do not say they are merely suspended, as in the previous halachah. It may be explained that since they were asked about the two sets of pure foods together, this case is treated like an impure loaf that got mixed into pure ones, where even one in a hundred makes them all impure and they are burned, as explained at the end of the halachah (see Mirkevet HaMishneh, who gave a different explanation, and see Tosafot Chadashim, Tahorot 5:5, who cited in the name of Maharash Chayim that in this case too the pure foods are suspended).
one impure. One who eats it becomes second-degree impure by rabbinic decree (see above 8:10).

because they are a doubt of rabbinic law, which falls among the doubtful cases the Sages declared pure. Since the impurity here is only rabbinic, its doubt is pure, even when the doubt is in a private domain (Melekhet Mishneh).
as we have explained. Above 15:1.

and their pure foods are burned, for certainly one of the sets of pure foods is impure. Even though the impurity of food that touched impure foods is only by rabbinic decree, we burn terumah because of it (see Mishnah Tahorot 1:3, and see Mishneh Achronah, Zavim 5:12).
an impure loaf that got mixed with nine pure loaves. Now all the loaves are considered impure and must be burned.
even if one of them was suspended. Doubtfully impure.
and we say: this pure one walked on the pure path, and he remains in his purity etc.. For something similar see also Hilchot Terumot 13:14, Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah 2:11.

any place that is a public domain etc.. Above 16:2 it was explained that if there are three people in a private domain it is treated as a public domain and its doubt is pure. This chapter details the places considered a public domain where, even when only one or two people are present, the doubt is pure since many people frequent them (see Rabbi Shimshon and Rosh, Tahorot 6:6).
a public domain with regard to Shabbat. For the definition of a public domain with regard to Shabbat see Hilchot Shabbat 14:1.
with regard to impurity. That the doubt of impurity in it is pure.
and likewise a karmelit. A domain that is not considered a private domain and not a public domain (for its definition see there, halachot 4-6).
and a colonnade. A roofed row of columns.
even though they are a private domain for Shabbat. For the definition of a private domain with regard to Shabbat see there, halachot 1-2.

paths that lead through to cisterns, pits, and winepresses. Passageways with partitions on both sides and an excavation in the ground at their end, so that they are closed on three sides and, with regard to Shabbat, are considered a private domain (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Tahorot 6:6).
in the summer days. When the workers are in the fields of the valley; but in the rainy season the valley is considered a private domain (below, halachah 6).
and a basilica. A palace.
the men of the chariot. The soldiers.
and the poran. A magnificent building (and see other explanations in Rabbi Shimshon, Tahorot 6:9).
alleys. Lanes.

even though they are fenced in on both sides and many people climb up through them. Even though they are surrounded by partitions, and for that reason are defined as a private domain with regard to Shabbat, since many people pass through them when coming up from the sea or the river, they are considered a public domain with regard to impurity.

and the bimosot. Palaces (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Avodah Zarah 1:7; and see Tosafot, Ritva, and other Rishonim there, 16b, some of whom read "dimosiyot," in which case it means healing springs).
the entire Temple court. In the Temple.

the gardens of the city through which the city road passes. In several manuscripts the reading here is "the roofs of the city," meaning that when a public road passes over the roofs, they are considered a public domain with regard to impurity (and see Torat Sefer Rishonim, Tahorot p. 79, which argues why this reading is accurate).
when it is guarded. That it is secured, for example when it has doors that are locked (Chazon Ish, Tahorot 7:11).
a public domain with regard to impurity. Although with regard to Shabbat it is still considered a private domain because it has partitions.

and likewise a large basilica when it is opened etc.. In contrast to a royal basilica, which is a public domain for impurity in every case (above, halachah 3), the basilica mentioned here is a public domain only when it is open.
in the rainy season. After it has been plowed and sown, when people do not enter it so as not to damage it.
and if it was not enclosed, it is a private domain for impurity only. But with regard to Shabbat it is like a karmelit (Hilchot Shabbat 14:4, Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Tahorot 6:7).

and a valley whose rainy season has passed etc.. A valley in which there was impurity during the rainy season, when it was defined as a private domain; even though the rainy season has passed and the summer has come, since it was established as a private domain with regard to that impurity, it remains in its presumption with regard to it (Rabbi Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 153b, and see the Rishonim there, who explained in other ways).
once the crops are removed from it. When anyone is permitted to enter there (Chazon Ish, Tahorot 7:8).
once the second rainfall has come. The second rainy period, from which time the seeds grow and trampling harms them (Tosafot, Bava Batra 153b, and see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:4).

between the grape rounds and the pressed skins etc.. The rounds are the vessels used when pressing wine from the grapes, and the pressed skins are the grape remains piled up in heaps; many people are found in this place since the pressing requires a large number of workers (see the commentators on the Mishnah, Tahorot 10:8).
a vineyard before the harvesters is a private domain. The part not yet harvested is considered a private domain, since the public may not enter there and eat from the grapes.
and after the harvesters is a public domain. For after the harvest the poor enter to gather the gifts for the poor.
when the public enters from this side and exits from the opposite side. As above, halachah 3, regarding a courtyard.
and the holes of a public domain. Holes in a wall that open onto a public domain.
even though they are not four by four. So they are not considered a private domain with regard to Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 14:10).

its doubt is pure, for the whole shop is like a creeping creature lying in a public domain. Even though the shop is a private domain, where a doubt of impurity is impure, since the person here stands outside the shop and is unsure whether he entered it and became impure or not, the doubt arose in a public domain and is therefore pure.
its doubt is impure, for this is a doubt in a private domain. For he certainly entered the private domain but does not know whether it was pure or impure.
and likewise a valley in the rainy season. Which is a private domain for impurity (above, halachah 6).

for a doubtful impurity in a private domain, even a doubt about entering, is impure. Since the person stands in the valley, the doubt arose in a private domain, and therefore even when the doubt is whether he entered the place of the impurity or not, its doubt is impure (Chatam Sofer, Bava Batra 55b).
a basket. A large basket.
ten handbreadths high. So that it itself is considered a private domain, as its height prevents the public from using it (Chazon Ish, Tahorot 7:2).

it is uncertain whether he touched or did not touch. That is, there is doubt whether he put his hand into the basket and touched the impurity or perhaps did not put in his hand at all, or, for example, the impurity protrudes outward and he is unsure whether he touched it (Rabbi Shimshon, Tahorot 6:3).
its doubt is pure. Since the doubt arose in a public domain.
he put his hand into it... its doubt is impure. Since he certainly put his hand into the basket, the doubt arose in a private domain.
a kefisha. A vessel that does not become impure.

and a loaf of terumah wrapped in bast or paper. Wrapped in threads or papers, which do not become impure; it is customary to keep terumah this way so that it does not become impure from ordinary hands, which are second-degree impure and disqualify terumah (Or Sameach).

if it is uncertain whether another person touched it or did not touch it, its doubt is impure. This refers to a case where the other person (whose hands are ordinarily impure) certainly put his hand into the kefisha (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon), since a kefisha placed on a person's shoulders is considered a private domain (as above 18:5 regarding spittle, Kesef Mishneh), and its doubt is impure even though the loaf is well protected by things that do not become impure.
he stretched his hand over his back... its doubt is impure. In such a case his hand lies in a private domain, whose doubt is impure.
this one was riding his donkey and that one was riding his donkey. One impure and one pure (Tosefta, Tahorot 7:5).
and the spittle was stuck to the wall. Even above ten handbreadths (see there), and spittle that is found is presumed impure.

all is pure. Although in all these cases both the impurity and the pure item are in a private domain, since the doubt arose while they were moving in a public domain and there is no single private domain common to both, its doubt is pure (see Ra'avad's commentary on Eduyot 3:7).
